notes.meaning: The men of the tribe of Ephraim gathered their army and crossed the Jordan River to the town of Zaphon. They were furious that Jephthah had defeated the Ammonites without inviting them to fight and share in the honor. Their wounded pride drove them to threaten to burn Jephthah's house down with him inside. Pride often blinds people and stirs up bitter quarrels with their own brothers.

Jephthah defended himself against their harsh words. He told them that he and his people had been in a desperate struggle with the Ammonites, and that he had called for Ephraim's help, but they refused to rescue him. Their complaint was dishonest because they only wanted praise after the danger had already passed.

Jephthah explained that when he saw Ephraim would not come, he risked his own life and marched against the enemy. Taking his life in his hands meant facing deadly danger with only his local volunteers. Since the Lord gave him the victory, Ephraim had no right to come and wage war against him.

Jephthah called together the men of Gilead to fight against Ephraim. The Gileadites were enraged because Ephraim had insulted them, calling them runaways and outcasts who had no real home. Cruel and mocking words quickly turned a family disagreement into a deadly civil war.

The Gileadites took control of the shallow crossing places along the Jordan River to block the Ephraimites from escaping home. Whenever a fleeing soldier tried to cross, the guards asked if he was an Ephraimite. The very men who had marched out in pride were now trapped and forced to hide who they were.

The guards tested each man by telling him to say "Shibboleth," a word meaning a stream of water. Because people from Ephraim had an accent that could not pronounce the "sh" sound, they said "Sibboleth" and gave themselves away. The Gileadites killed every man who failed the test, and in all, forty-two thousand Ephraimites fell in that conflict.

Jephthah served as judge over Israel for six years before he died. He was buried in his home region in one of the cities of Gilead. Even leaders whom God uses to win great battles must eventually face death and the grave.

After Jephthah died, a man named Ibzan became the next judge over Israel. He lived in the town of Bethlehem and guided the nation during a time of rest. God provided steady leadership to keep the tribes at peace.

Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters, showing that he was a wealthy and influential leader. He arranged marriages for all of his daughters outside his clan and brought in thirty wives for his sons to build peaceful alliances. He led Israel faithfully for seven years.

Ibzan died after seven years of leadership and was buried in his hometown of Bethlehem. His quiet life left behind a record of peace rather than war. A life lived in quiet usefulness is a great gift from the Lord.

After Ibzan died, Elon from the northern tribe of Zebulun became Israel's next judge. He governed the people and upheld justice for ten years. God continued to raise up leaders from different tribes across the land.

Elon died after ten years of serving as judge over the nation. He was buried at Aijalon in his home territory of Zebulun. The Bible honors his memory by recording his faithful service and his final resting place.

After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel from the town of Pirathon became the next judge of Israel. He was from the tribe of Ephraim and was called to guide the nation during a time of calm. God continued to give his people leaders to protect them from chaos.

Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy young donkeys. Riding donkeys was a sign of wealth and high rank in Israel, showing that his large family served as respected leaders. He judged Israel in peace for eight years.

Abdon died after eight years of leading Israel and was buried in his hometown of Pirathon in the land of Ephraim. His peaceful burial in his own land brought an end to his leadership. Even the most prosperous and honored rulers eventually return to the dust.
